reading.body:
AI litigation is being decided on precedents that predate generative models, not on new law written for them.

The structure of the field is two layers. One is a live docket layer, case pages for AI lawsuits in United States courts refreshed daily from CourtListener. The other is a precedent layer, the older decisions the current cases are actually argued out of. The named precedents are Sony on substantial non-infringing use, Campbell and Google Books on transformative purpose, Van Buren and hiQ on scraping, and Zeran on Section 230. Copyright, scraping and defamation cases all draw from that same small set.

This matters for AI because the legal risk around models is not being resolved by statutes aimed at models. It is being resolved by how far older doctrines stretch. Training data disputes turn on transformative purpose and substantial non-infringing use. Data acquisition disputes turn on scraping doctrine. Output disputes turn on Section 230. The compute buildout proceeds on the assumption that these questions have answers, and the answers are being produced case by case in ordinary courts.

What this does not cover is the substance of any ruling. There are no case names beyond the precedents, no parties, no holdings, no dates, and no count of active suits. The tracker is described as refreshed daily, but nothing here reports what it currently contains. Treat this as a map of where AI litigation lives and what it rests on, not as a status report on it.
